sources.headline: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
sources.text: After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap."I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised fist clenching a red bra.The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet? Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter."Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology. State governments could also launch their own investigations.Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself."I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X."Congress has much to investigate," he said.While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed. Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large. In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption."Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year. The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules."It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday. "Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy. He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic). And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters. He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%. Last Friday alone, it fell 14%. US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed. And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

Huang's return fails to dispel doubts as Nvidia shares drop

Issued on: 25/11/2026 - 17:24

A rally sparked by Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia's chief executive faded on Tuesday, with the company's shares falling as doubts persisted over the probes he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom. After vaulting more than 30 percent on Monday following Huang's shock comeback, Nvidia fell almost six percent Tuesday. Huang resigned on November 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

sources.headline: Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief
sources.text:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., on Nvidia CEO's upcoming House committee interview
Transcript

Transcript
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., speaks at a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee hearing in Washington on Sept. 21, 2022.
Samuel Corum/Getty Images
hide caption
Samuel Corum/Getty Images
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled. U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing. There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.
Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached. Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week. For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats. "What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked. Huang's reinstatement, Fitzpatrick said, should not put those questions to rest. "The public is rightly concerned, and they deserve answers," he said. Fitzpatrick also wants to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche, who on Tuesday described Nvidia as a good corporate citizen, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department faces questions over Nvidia's chip exports to China. "Anytime you do an investigation, you follow the facts wherever they lead, and you report those facts with unimpeachable integrity," Fitzpatrick said. "You leave no stone unturned." The debate over Huang's reinstatement extends beyond Washington.
In Silicon Valley, his return has alarmed women and advocates who have spent years pushing for a better workplace culture, renewing questions about the limits of executive accountability. Listen to the full interview by clicking on the blue button above. The radio interview was edited by Ally Schweitzer.

US ⁠officials found no evidence ⁠that tech executive Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with a classified briefing.

The briefing ‌comes after US President Donald Trump cleared the way for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement earlier this week, assuring Nvidia that its CEO posed no national-security threat.

The controversy began with concerns over Alice Huang’s alleged Chinese intelligence links and whether her relationship with Jensen Huang affected suspected diversions ⁠of Nvidia chips to China.

Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director ‌of National Intelligence and National Security Agency briefed staff from congressional intelligence committees and chamber leaders, the Journal reported.

The officials said ‌Alice Huang contacted China’s spy agency during the affair but found ⁠no indication ⁠that she provided significant intelligence, the Journal reported.

Nvidia and the agencies did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report.

Shares of Nvidia tumbled more ‌than 7 per cent, ‌putting the chipmaker on track to shed more than US$250 billion in ‌market value and eroding a 31 per cent comeback rally after CEO Huang’s reinstatement that ⁠added over US$900 billion.

The report said current evidence suggests that Alice Huang and Jensen ⁠Huang may have had an amorous relationship, but not a coordinated play by China, adding that new information could, however, change that ‌assessment.

The briefing also noted ‌that Kang Wei, described to the Journal as Alice Huang’s husband by people who know them, was an asset for China’s Ministry of State Security who remained in frequent contact with the intelligence service.

sources.headline: US Justice Department did not open probe into Jensen Huang before reinstatement, sources say
sources.text: WASHINGTON - The US Justice Department did not conduct a formal investigation into Jensen Huang before US President Donald Trump pushed for his return as Nvidia chief executive this week, despite active probes into the chipmaker’s customers and allegations he conducted an affair with a woman linked to Chinese intelligence, according to three people familiar with the matter.Instead, Attorney-General Todd Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws based on the Justice Department's ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.That determination, which is subject to change as the probes continue, was crucial to Blanche’s decision to tell Trump and Vice-President J.D. Vance over the weekend that he possessed no evidence that Huang posed a risk to national security, said two of the people.Jensen Huang’s reinstatement has angered members of Congress - both Republicans and Democrats - who say it’s too soon to set aside questions about whether Nvidia or its CEO endangered US national security. The lack of any additional effort to examine their roles prior to Trump’s intervention will likely fuel a push for more investigations on Capitol Hill.Huang is due to testify next week.The Justice Department probes of Nvidia customers found no evidence that Huang was acting as an agent of China or knowingly transferred sensitive semiconductor technology or information to China, the two people said. Nvidia was not a target of those investigations and cooperated, providing documents, interviews and other data that helped lead to that conclusion, they added.There was also no counterintelligence probe of Huang himself. US spy agencies have gathered information on Alice Huang - the former Megaspeed executive and alleged paramour of Jensen Huang suspected of working with Chinese intelligence - said two other people familiar with the effort. But the US had no details that would warrant a probe into the Nvidia CEO, they said.Counterintelligence investigations are run separately from criminal investigations and are aimed at monitoring and neutralising national security threats, rather than building a case for indictment.Justice Department officials concluded that Nvidia and Huang had committed no wrongdoing and did not suspect its chief executive posed a national-security risk, two of the people familiar with the matter said.Trump and Vance conveyed that conclusion to Nvidia’s board, which decided to reinstate Huang, according to Trump’s account of events in a CNBC interview on Nov 23.‘Good corporate citizen’Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Nov 12 following allegations he conducted affairs with Alice Huang and at least two employees. Jensen Huang acknowledged infidelities but has not confirmed his involvement with Alice Huang specifically.Reuters has been unable to reach her or confirm her links to Chinese spy services.Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Trump in May about the affair, according to the New York Times.The Times also reported that Alice Huang was in touch with a top Chinese spy official for more than a year during the affair.Blanche said following Huang’s departure that the FBI was “looking into” reports that he was having an affair with a spy, but had not reached any conclusions.At a press conference on Nov 24, Blanche repeatedly declined to answer questions about how the Trump administration determined that Huang was not a threat to US national security.He said he had found no evidence that Nvidia engaged in wrongdoing.“I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything other than a good corporate citizen,” he said at the press conference.The Justice Department is also conducting antitrust reviews of Nvidia business deals unrelated to Huang’s personal behaviour.A Justice Department spokesperson referred questions to Blanche’s statement, and a DOJ official previously told Reuters that no evidence of wrongdoing has been found. The FBI and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not respond to requests for comment.The Wall Street Journal first reported that Blanche’s assessment was based on evidence from the two related investigations.Defensive briefingsExperts said the federal officials bypassed standard counterintelligence protocols.“No formal Justice Department investigation into the national security allegations has been reported. That’s alarming, if unsurprising,” said Steve Cash, a former CIA officer who heads The Steady State, an association of former national security officials.The FBI has provided at least two “defensive briefings” to Nvidia leadership regarding Chinese espionage tactics, according to a law enforcement official familiar with the briefings, who spoke on condition of anonymity.It was not clear whether those briefings, which have not been previously reported, were standard security engagements routinely provided to major American technology firms, or focused specifically on the threat posed by Alice Huang. It also was not clear whether Huang himself was briefed.Federal officials often deliver broad warnings to US companies about espionage risks, two former senior law enforcement officials told Reuters.Defensive briefings can lead to a criminal inquiry if the warnings are ignored, said Kevin Carroll, a former undercover CIA operations officer, but their main purpose is to protect national security. REUTERS
